courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drain: a fixed-depth parse tree and a similarity threshold
md: The one thing to remember: Drain bounds the work per line to a fixed tree walk plus a comparison against the few groups in one leaf, which makes its cost $O(n)$ in the number of lines. It buys that speed with two assumptions, that same-template lines share a token count and that early tokens are constants.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
md: A Windows 4625 converted to ECS and an sshd failure converted to ECS look identical to a rule, which is the point, but also a risk: a mapping mistake (say, putting the target host into source.ip) now breaks every rule at once. Test mappings with sample events from each source, exactly like rules (lesson 11).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
md: State's advantage was not a product; it was three years of studying normal mailbox access, which let a modest-looking event stand out. The CSRB notes that buying the logs alone would not have been enough: few organisations analysed that voluminous log in detail.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Other routes to long context: base scaling, searched factors, data
md: Long data alone was not enough. Xiong et al. report that with Llama 2's original base the model still could not attend effectively beyond about 4,000 to 6,000 tokens after extensive long-context continual pretraining. Changing the base of a finished model without training, on the other hand, is just NTK-aware scaling with a huge s. The knob and the training go together.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Extending RoPE (PI, NTK, YaRN) makes long positions *in distribution*; Ring Attention and context parallelism make long sequences *fit*; neither guarantees the model *uses* the context. Measure effective length with depth-controlled tasks such as RULER.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
md: Everything here is one seed of a 219K-parameter model on a synthetic task. Treat the numbers as a demonstration of the mechanism (more iterations resolve deeper chains, exits track depth, starts are forgotten), not as evidence about which adapter is better at scale.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA = frozen W0 + (alpha/r) B A, with B initialized to zero. You train r times (d + k) numbers per adapted matrix, and the model starts exactly at the pretrained one.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: Low scores on forget benchmarks show suppressed outputs, not erased knowledge. Small fine-tunes, probes and even 4-bit quantization can bring "forgotten" knowledge back, because approximate unlearning moves the weights only slightly.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Notarization, revocation and the Shlayer lesson
md: Notarization means "Apple's automated scan found nothing known-bad when this was uploaded". It is not a review of intent, and it can be fooled by code that only turns malicious later or hides its payload. Its real strength is speed of revocation once something is reported.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Case: Atomic Stealer and the paste-into-Terminal era
md: Resetting the user's password is not enough after a stealer. Session cookies stolen from the browser let the attacker into SaaS apps without the password or MFA until those sessions are revoked server-side.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The PE format: headers, sections and what imports reveal
md: Our benign hello.exe imports VirtualProtect and VirtualQuery even though main never calls them: the MinGW-w64 C runtime's startup code uses them. One 'suspicious' import proves nothing. Read imports as a combination, and check what the compiler's runtime adds.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Writing and testing YARA rules
md: A YARA rule is a hypothesis about what makes a family unique. The test set is the evidence. Keep the test files and expected results next to the rule, and rerun them on every change, just like unit tests.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number
md: Savings multiply, but so do quality losses. Each step (fewer dims, fewer bits) costs some recall, and the costs compound. Measure recall on your own queries at the exact size and precision you plan to serve, then use a rerank stage (next lesson) to win most of it back.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: The 5as/h term assumes attention materializes the s x s score matrix. Fused attention kernels (FlashAttention, Dao et al. 2022, which computes attention tile by tile in fast on-chip memory; also in NVIDIA's Transformer Engine library) never store it, so most of that term disappears by itself. Megatron Core's config even warns that with fused attention there is no need to put core_attn in --recompute-modules.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Hands on: plan, launch, profile and checkpoint an MCore run
md: Plan with the formulas (state, activations, bubble), launch with flags that encode the plan, measure MFU against a named peak, profile for exposed communication and bubbles, and checkpoint in a format you can reshard.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Handles, mutexes, sockets and registry hives in memory
md: Every network row in memory names its owning process, and every handle names its holder. That pairing (this PID talked to that address, this PID opened that process) is what turns a list of artefacts into an attribution inside the host.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
md: `sizeof` is not what you pay. With a million 130-byte records you might budget 124 MiB, but jemalloc hands out 160 bytes each (153 MiB) and a power-of-two allocator 256 (244 MiB). Measure with `malloc_usable_size` or allocator stats, not by multiplying `sizeof`.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: Synchronization needs a pair on the same atomic: a Release (or stronger) write and an Acquire (or stronger) read that observes that write or its release sequence. Then everything before the write is visible after the read.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU protects readers from updaters, not updaters from each other. `rcu_assign_pointer()` does not make two concurrent updates safe; the example still takes `foo_mutex`. And a pointer from `rcu_dereference()` is valid only inside the critical section that fetched it.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Heap overflow: corrupting the neighbouring object
md: A heap overflow damages whoever happens to be next, and you cannot predict who that is: it depends on the allocator, the sizes and the order of allocations. Treat any heap overflow as able to corrupt any nearby object.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
md: Hard is not the same as useful. The very hardest negatives in a large dataset are often mislabeled or badly imaged examples (FaceNet names both). Training only on them teaches the network to fit noise.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
md: A microbenchmark's working set and access pattern are part of the experiment. Report them next to the time, and sweep the size if the code's data can be large.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Launching and watching a Miles run
md: A Miles launch script is the recipe of record: read its options table and `EXEC:` lines to know what ran, override with `--extra-args` (the last flag wins), and keep lasting changes in the script. Judge the run against the monitoring table, telling a one-time jump in logprob diff from a climb.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Bitwise-equal logprobs do not make an async run on-policy. True-on-policy alignment removes numerical mismatch between engines, not staleness from training on groups generated under older weights; the data buffer bounds that separately.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Reported speedups are relative to specific baselines on specific traces: B-LRU on six CDN traces, a tuned weighted fair scheduler on TPC-H mixes, a read-optimized B-tree on read-only integer keys. A different workload, or a stronger baseline, can shrink the gain to zero.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Content providers and shared files: from URI grants to Dirty Stream
md: A shared file arrives with two attacker-controlled things: its content and its name. Treat both as untrusted input. Choose your own name, and parse the content as hostile.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
md: MLA is not a compression applied to an already trained model's cache, like PCA (principal component analysis, which finds the few directions that capture most of the variation in a set of vectors) run on stored keys. The down- and up-projections are ordinary weights learned from scratch during pretraining. Converting an existing MHA or GQA model to MLA needs extra fine-tuning work (see lesson 7).

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Unmerged does not mean easy. Requests in one batch use adapters with different ranks and different sequence lengths, so padding everything into one batched matmul wastes work. S-LoRA's variant that copies adapters into contiguous memory and uses padded batched matmul (S-LoRA-bmm) was much slower than the version with custom kernels, GPU functions written for exactly this mixed-rank job.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Build it and size it: a mixed-adapter layer and a capacity plan
md: "Power-law popularity with exponent alpha" means different things in different papers. S-LoRA's alpha = 1 is uniform, Punica's Zipf-1.5 makes each adapter 1.5 times as popular as the next, and this lesson's Zipf exponent 1 gives the top adapter 14.7%. Compare results only after converting to the same quantity, such as the top-10 share.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Use multi-query when recall is the bottleneck because users word things differently from the corpus, and the next stage can absorb more candidates. Skip it for precise lookups, compound questions (decompose instead), tight latency budgets, and pipelines where a fixed reranker budget already decides the outcome. Measure end-to-end, not just first-stage recall.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon does not produce an exactly orthogonal matrix. The reference implementation's docstring says the result is closer to $US'V^\top$ with the entries of $S'$ roughly uniform in $[0.5, 1.5]$, and that this does not hurt model performance. The Moonlight team also found 10 steps gave a more accurate result than 5 but no better training.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muTransfer has three steps: parametrize the target in muP, tune a smaller version of it, copy the tuned HPs to the target. It works because muP makes the optimal HPs converge to fixed values as width grows.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: muTransfer in practice: what transfers and what it saved
md: Don't expect dropout or weight decay tuned on a small proxy to be optimal for a much larger model trained on different amounts of data. The paper also notes that muTransfer may not be enough for fine-tuning on small datasets, where regularization matters most.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
md: `spin_loop()` is not `yield` (such as Rust's `std::thread::yield_now()`, which asks the operating system scheduler to run another thread for now). It is a hint to the CPU, not to the scheduler: a thread spinning with it still occupies the CPU for its whole time slice.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Snapshots: how each transaction picks its version
md: Visibility is decided at read time by comparing tuple stamps against the reader's snapshot. Changing *when* the snapshot is taken changes what a transaction sees, without touching the data.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
md: An NER system is three pieces that must agree with each other: a **tag set** that can represent any set of non-overlapping spans, a **model** that scores tag sequences, and a **decoder** that turns tags back into spans. Most NER bugs live in the seams between them, not in the model.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Who runs them: services, commands, contractors and fronts
md: A company named in an indictment is not proof that all of its work is state-directed, nor that a state ordered a particular intrusion. DOJ itself says i-Soon worked both on request and "on its own initiative", and that charges are allegations until proven in court.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: What the war showed, and what is still argued about
md: Both "cyber war turned out to be hype" and "cyber decided the war" overclaim. The public record is partial: most operations and most defensive successes are classified or unpublished. State which source a conclusion comes from, what data it rests on, and whether its author calls it a finding or a hypothesis.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Write NSA and DSA as masked attention and test them against dense
md: Write the masked reference first. Setting the sparsity knob to select everything must reproduce dense attention exactly, and any fast kernel can then be compared with the reference on random inputs, including its gradients.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
md: NeMo RL separates *what the algorithm does* (a single-controller loop written as if on one GPU) from *where it runs* (RayVirtualCluster plus RayWorkerGroups). Swapping vLLM for another engine, or changing GPU counts, should not change the algorithm code.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DHCP starvation and rogue DHCP servers
md: Whoever answers DHCP chooses a device's gateway and DNS server, so a rogue DHCP server is an on-path attack on every device it reaches. Only trusted ports may send DHCP server messages.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Segmentation, zero trust and the Target breach
md: Segmentation limits how far one compromise spreads; zero trust removes network location as a reason to trust anything. Both assume a breach will happen, and both only pay off when someone watches the alerts at the boundaries.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: What TLS still reveals, and fingerprinting clients with JA3
md: A fingerprint identifies a TLS library and its configuration, not an intention. Python, Go and Windows programs share fingerprints with malware written in the same language or on the same stack. Use JA3 to cluster and to rank leads, never as a verdict on its own.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
md: Every packet is a header plus a payload. Every device on the path must read the header to deliver it, and can read the payload too unless it is encrypted. Both facts drive almost everything in network security.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
md: TLS protects the content of one connection between two endpoints. It does not hide who talks to whom, it does not make the server trustworthy, and it does not protect data once it is decrypted at either end.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Policy = mode + nodes + scope, applied at allocation time. Use bind for strict isolation, preferred when spilling over is acceptable, interleave for big shared data, and leave private per-thread data on the default local policy.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
md: A detector outputs a variable-size set of (box, class, score) triples, and IoU between boxes is the measure every later stage builds on.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: Pick the counting method by scene: detection when objects are separable and you need locations, density maps for dense crowds where boxes fail, and tracking plus line or region events for video, where the same object appears in many frames.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Never compute a rate as last value minus first value over a counter. One restart in the window turns a positive rate into a large negative number, and `rate()` exists precisely to handle that case for you.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: OCR is a chain: detect, then recognize, then order and extract. Each stage only sees the previous stage's output, so an early error silently becomes a wrong field later.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
md: User programs run in ring 3 and can only ask; the kernel runs in ring 0 and decides. A system call is the only door between them. Sandboxing is mostly the art of closing doors and narrowing what each open door accepts.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Sandboxes: Chrome's broker model, macOS and iOS
md: A broker is only as good as its request checking. A broker that performs "open this path" for any path a renderer names has turned itself into a tool for the attacker. That failure has a name, the confused deputy, and it is the subject of lesson 15.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Your own footprint while investigating: OPSEC and bias
md: Investigating leaves traces. Use a separate, logged-out research environment, expect the other side to read its logs, and record your exact queries because results differ by engine, location and history.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
md: List clues, bound the area, eliminate candidates with the most distinctive clue first, then confirm with an independent feature. Report what matched and what could not be checked.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise
md: An ethical OSINT engagement is authorised, planned, minimal, preserved, verified and reported with its limits, and it ends with fixes and deleted working data.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: CI is a contract written in the repo: on these events, on these machines, run these commands, and block the merge unless they exit with status 0. Read `.github/workflows/` before your first PR to a project.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Misconception: a reviewer who leaves 15 comments is blocking you on all 15. Often most are optional. If the reviewer did not say which ones block the merge, ask instead of guessing.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: Read in this order before you touch code: LICENSE (can you contribute at all), CONTRIBUTING (how), CODE_OF_CONDUCT (how to behave), SECURITY (if your finding is a vulnerability). Ten minutes of reading avoids a rejected PR.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebase rewrites history. The rule from Pro Git, the free Git book on git-scm.com: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on. Your own PR branch is the usual exception, which is why the next lesson's force-push needs care, not a ban.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: Public is not the same as open source. Code you can read on GitHub with no license file is all rights reserved, and so is a snippet whose license you never checked.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: CLA: one signed agreement per person or company, granting rights up front. DCO: no agreement, just a per-commit certification of origin via Signed-off-by, checked mechanically by email match.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
md: A common mistake is to fix a bug inside a generated file. Your edit is overwritten the next time the generator runs, and reviewers will reject it. When a file says *do not edit*, find its input (here `src/commands/get.json`) in the build rule and change that instead.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: Every cut is an experiment: remove, rerun, compare to the original failure. Keep cuts that preserve the exact error; undo the rest.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: If the project squash-merges PRs, your intermediate commits disappear from the main branch anyway, and the PR as a whole becomes one commit. That makes **one logical change per PR** even more important: the squash cannot separate a fix from a speedup after the fact.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths (the next lesson shows where those come from). It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Longest-prefix-first can starve a request whose prefix is never cached, since others keep jumping ahead. The SGLang paper says so and leaves fair scheduling as future work.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: certificate logs, search engines and leaked code
md: A leaked password or API key found during recon is not an invitation to log in with it. Unless the rules of engagement explicitly allow using discovered credentials, record where it was found and report it at once so it can be rotated.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: Colors carry no meaning in a default CPU flame graph. Gregg picks random warm colors only to separate neighbors. Other palettes exist (for example coloring kernel, user and just-in-time (JIT) frames differently, where JIT code is machine code that a runtime such as the Java virtual machine compiles while the program runs), but never read hotness from hue.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
md: A fence without a flush does nothing for durability on ADR platforms, and a flush without a fence gives no ordering: CLWB and CLFLUSHOPT are not ordered with each other or with later stores. You need both, in the order store, flush, fence, then the dependent store.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: DMARC: alignment, policy and reports
md: Misconception: "we have DMARC, so we are protected from phishing". DMARC at p=reject stops exact-domain spoofing of **your** domain. It does nothing against lookalike domains, display-name spoofs or a compromised real mailbox, and p=none stops nothing at all; it only reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
md: Do not reorder blindly. If a struct's layout is part of a file format, a network protocol, a hardware register map or an ABI shared with other code, changing the order changes the bytes and breaks every reader. Reordering is safe only for structs that are private to one build of your program.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding
md: The network never outputs coordinates. It outputs heatmaps, and a small hand-written decoder (argmax, quarter-cell shift, scale by stride, undo the crop) turns them into numbers. Bugs in that decoder, such as swapping x and y or forgetting the crop offset, look like a bad model.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Encrypting one bit with LWE, by hand
md: This toy exists to make the math visible. Never write your own lattice cryptography for real use: use ML-KEM from a maintained library (lesson 8), whose implementers also handle constant-time code, input checks and randomness.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Do not read 3% as a safe threshold. Proximity graphs are not random graphs, matching nodes are often clustered, and being connected is weaker than being *navigable*: greedy search can stall in a matching region long before the subgraph formally splits. Qdrant's docs simply warn that the HNSW graph starts to fall apart when filters are too strict.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: Common misconception: "faster RAM will speed up my tree or hash-chain lookups." Faster transfer rates raise peak bandwidth, but a dependent chain of misses uses a tiny fraction of it. Its cost is set by latency, which has improved far more slowly.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Pseudonyms and hashes are not anonymity: AOL 2006
md: Pseudonyms protect the name, not the person. They link all of one person's records, and those records (queries, routes, purchases) can identify them by content. Ask what a released record says, not only what field was deleted.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
md: Differential privacy is a property of the mechanism: on any two datasets differing in one person, every output is at most e^epsilon times likelier on one than the other. It survives post-processing and any auxiliary data, and epsilons add up across releases.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
md: Minimise by architecture: collect less, coarsen at the edge, compute on the device, separate identity from content, enforce purposes in the access layer and in database grants, and default to the least sharing.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
md: Rights are requirements on every copy: build a data map (system, lookup key, export method, erase method), meet the one-month clock (Art. 12(3)), put backups beyond use, notify recipients, and verify identity in proportion to what you would hand over.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Defending the path: segmentation, admin hygiene, EDR, HSE timeline
md: Escalation and lateral movement are a chain of small, valid-looking steps. Make each step harder (least privilege, unique and protected credentials, segmentation, patching known-exploited bugs) and make each step visible (forwarded logs, EDR, the event chains in this course), then make sure every alert has an owner.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
md: Same scores, three uses: rerank finished solutions (weighted voting is a strong default), prune partial solutions in beam search (best on harder problems at modest budgets), or provide step-level rewards so RL can credit each step separately.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
md: Misconception: "nice 19 means it only runs when the machine is idle." A nice 19 task still has weight 15, so against one nice 0 task it gets about 1.4 percent. For truly leftover CPU, use the `SCHED_IDLE` policy, which the CFS document describes as even weaker than nice 19.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes
md: Raising code size cannot fix a too-small nprobe. The paper notes that increasing the code length is useless if w is not big enough, because neighbors outside the probed lists are never scored. Tune nprobe first, then code size.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Any structural comparison in this field is after optimal superposition. A reported RMSD of 1.4 Angstrom always means 1.4 after Kabsch alignment; the unaligned number is meaningless because it depends on where the coordinates happen to be written down.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Regular expressions: counting failed logins per address
md: A per-address threshold is easy to evade. Mandiant saw UNC5537 log in mostly through commercial VPN (virtual private network) addresses, and stuffing tools can spread attempts so each address fails only once or twice. Also count failures per username, and treat any success after failures as more important than the failures themselves.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Testing your script so it does not fail silently
md: Test the awkward inputs and the failure paths, not just the happy path, and keep tests offline with fakes. A test suite is what lets you change a detection script without wondering what you broke.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: LLM expansion prompts, and deciding per query whether to expand
md: Predicting which queries expansion will help is hard; simple score-based gates tuned on dev did not transfer to test here. Gates that do hold are rules about the query itself: never expand quoted phrases, exact identifiers (part numbers, error codes, SKUs) or field-restricted queries, because there the user's exact string is the point.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: The rotation does not make every vector quantize well on every draw. It makes the quality *random with a known distribution*, the same for every input direction. That is what turns "works on my dataset" into a guarantee that holds regardless of the data.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Discounts, refunds and rewards: value that can be claimed twice
md: Evaluate every reward rule against the final state of the transaction, at the moment value moves, and record each grant so it cannot be granted again. A rule checked earlier is a rule that can go stale.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
md: "It is in a transaction" is not a race fix by itself. At Read Committed, a SELECT then an UPDATE in one transaction still race. You need a lock, a conditional write, a constraint, or SERIALIZABLE with retries.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work
md: Majorities intersect. Every safety argument in Paxos and Raft comes down to one server that sat in both quorums and remembered what it saw.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Top-k, the token budget, and where chunks sit in the prompt
md: Three separate decisions shape the context: **how many** chunks (top-k), **how many tokens** they may use (the budget, set by the window minus everything else), and **in what order** they appear. Tune them together; raising k without a budget or an ordering rule mostly adds noise to the middle.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: **Recall@k is not Success@k.** Some papers report "Recall@k" meaning *at least one relevant document is in the top k*. The ir_measures documentation calls that **Success@k** and reserves R@k for the fraction of all relevant documents retrieved. For q1 every run has Success@5 = 1, while R@5 ranges from 0.167 to 0.667. Check which one a paper means before comparing numbers.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Extortion layers: encryption, theft, leak sites and pressure
md: Backups defeat encryption only. Stolen data is lost the moment it leaves, so treat exfiltration detection as part of ransomware defence, and prepare the communication that answers a leak-site post before one appears.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Recovery sequencing: identity first, then the business
md: Recover in dependency order: a clean network, then the independent backup system, then identity restored in isolation from a pre-attack backup with privileged secrets reset, then security tooling, then business services by a critical asset list agreed before the incident.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
md: Masking is **not encryption**: the key travels in the same frame. RFC 6455 requires it (even over TLS) so that a script in the browser cannot choose the exact bytes on the wire. Without it, an attacker could craft upgraded traffic that a broken proxy reads as an HTTP request and caches, then serves that forged response to other users: the cache-poisoning attack in section 10.3. Use `wss://` (TLS) for confidentiality.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Item-to-item CF scales because the heavy work (the similar-items table) is offline, and the online step only touches the handful of items in one user's history.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why a photo has no scale until you add a reference
md: A reference object gives you scale only for points at its depth (more precisely, on its plane). Everything else in the image has a different pixels-per-mm.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The same study found that most of PostgreSQL's timeouts came from a nested-loop join without an index, chosen because a tiny row estimate made it look cheapest. When the real input was large, its rows x rows work exploded. A cost-only choice ignores how risky a plan is if the estimate is wrong.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: The reward is an imperfect measurement of the goal. Optimization pressure flows to wherever the measurement and the goal disagree, so the harder you optimize, the more those disagreements decide what you get.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: From gaming to tampering: reward tampering and in-context hacking
md: Gaming generalizes. A model rewarded for easy, harmless-looking gaming became more likely to try rarer and more blatant gaming it was never trained on, and training away only the gaming you can see leaves some of the rest.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
md: Monte Carlo is not magic: garbage ranges give precise-looking garbage. The model also assumes the factors are independent (here, a bad attack year does not make secondary losses bigger), which may not hold. Show your inputs with the outputs, say what is assumed, and rerun when estimates change. Simplified: real FAIR tools also model multiple loss forms separately and correlations between factors.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
md: ISO 27001 certifies a management system: risk assessment, treatment, a Statement of Applicability against 93 Annex A controls, internal audit, management review, continual improvement. Certificates last three years with yearly surveillance. The SoA and your risk register are the documents everything else hangs from.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Breach notification clocks and US disclosure rules
md: Know your clocks before the incident: NIS2 24 h and 72 h, GDPR 72 h from awareness, SEC four business days from a materiality decision made without unreasonable delay, state laws often 30 to 60 days, HIPAA at most 60 days. Encryption is an exemption almost everywhere. Prepare templates and decision owners in the incident plan.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: Rollout is the bottleneck. FLOPs are dominated by training, but wall-clock time is dominated by sequential decoding. Most RL infrastructure ideas (fast inference engines, placement, resharding, asynchrony, partial rollouts) are ways to make generation faster or to keep the other GPUs busy while it runs.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
md: Asynchrony converts idle GPU time into staleness. Every async system pairs a staleness bound (versions tracked per trajectory) with an objective that knows which policy sampled each token: an importance weight from behavior to proximal policy, and a trust region around a recent policy.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute
md: Read the gaps. In the NERSC study of DeepCAM (a deep learning model that finds extreme weather patterns in climate images), a kernel whose L1, L2 and HBM points sit close together shows a streaming pattern with poor cache locality; a large gap between the L2 and HBM points shows that L2 misses were rare. The binding level is the one whose roof is lowest at that level's own intensity.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: At the default k = 60 with typical windows (tens of results), RRF behaves like a vote count first (how many lists returned the document) and uses ranks mainly to order documents with the same count. Smaller k gives ranks more say; larger k makes it closer to pure vote counting.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Unsafe code is concentrated in reviewed subsystem abstractions. A driver written only against those abstractions cannot cause undefined behavior, *provided the abstractions are sound* and every `unsafe` block honours its contract. That proviso is the whole game; lesson 10 shows what happens when it fails.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: What Rust in the kernel does not prevent, and what it costs
md: Misconception: "written in Rust" means "free of memory corruption". A soundness bug in one `unsafe` block can corrupt memory exactly like C. What changes is *where to look*: the bug was in an unsafe block with a written, checkable claim, not anywhere in thousands of lines of driver logic.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: Weighted vtime in sched_ext takes a few lines: order a custom DSQ by vtime, charge `used x 100 / weight` in `stopping`, and cap how far behind a waking task's vtime may be. Whether the weights actually hold depends on whether prev competes in `dispatch`; `scx_simple`'s does not, so on one CPU no task gets more than half.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production
md: Ignoring kernel bugs, the kernel's tools/sched_ext README puts the worst case plainly: a broken sched_ext scheduler can starve some threads until the watchdog fires. It cannot corrupt memory, and the machine returns to the fair scheduler on its own.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key hierarchies in KMS: envelope encryption and rotating the KEK
md: Two different jobs share the word rotation. Rotating a KEK limits the amount of data under one key version and lets old versions eventually be retired. Revoking access (permissions, sessions, leases) is what stops a thief. Plan both.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: eval, pickle and yaml.load turn data into code
md: Pickle shows up in places reviewers forget: cache layers, task queues, session stores, and machine learning model files, which are often pickles inside. "It only comes from our own cache" is true only until someone else can write to that cache.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Go: nil maps, data races and the race detector
md: Go is memory-safe only for race-free programs. In every diff, find state shared between goroutines (globals, maps in structs, caches) and confirm one lock or channel owns it. Run tests with -race, and remember it only sees the paths your tests execute.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: White-box review of a small app, end to end
md: A baseline review is the four questions applied systematically: list every entry point, check authentication and authorization on each, trace every input to every sink, then sweep the language's hazards. Tools find the dangerous calls; only the reviewer finds the missing checks.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: When the state machine forgets: Erlang/OTP SSH (CVE-2025-32433)
md: Default deny applies to protocol states as much as to firewall rules: for each state, list the messages that are allowed and reject everything else. A dispatcher that looks only at the message type is an authentication bypass waiting for someone to send messages out of order.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Clark-Wilson: well-formed transactions and separation of duty
md: Giving a reporting job or an engineer direct write access to production tables quietly turns them into an uncertified TP. Read-only replicas for reporting, and audited break-glass access for emergencies, keep rule E1 true.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024
md: Mitigation is not remediation. Volexity's disclosure warned that a mitigation "does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise". After an edge device is exploited, assume its secrets and its users' credentials are gone, and rotate them.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Testing and running automations: dry runs, caps and staged rollout
md: Put validation, never-act lists, caps, idempotency and dry run inside the action function; test the failure paths and hostile inputs; roll out in stages; and alert when an automation goes quiet.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
md: Before asking "is this secure?", ask "which asset, and which property: confidentiality, integrity or availability?" Different properties need different defences: encryption (scrambling data so only holders of a secret key can read it) mostly protects confidentiality, hashes and signatures protect integrity and authenticity, and backups and redundancy protect availability.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
md: The leak did not create the vulnerability; it created a free, reliable exploit. By the time WannaCry hit, the patch had existed for 59 days. Treat every critical advisory as if working exploit code will be public soon, because sometimes it already is.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
md: Authorisation is the line. Own it or get written, scoped permission; stop at other people's data; report privately and give owners time to fix. Practise on platforms built for it.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Prioritising a portfolio: expected loss removed per dollar
md: Rank by expected loss removed per dollar, check combinations when options are few, fund obligations and foundations first, test whether the decision survives changes to the shakiest estimate, and hand every unfunded risk back to its owner in writing.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Leading through a major incident: the executive layer
md: The commonest executive failure is not a wrong technical call; it is delay while waiting for certainty, or deciding in a side conversation that nobody records. Both later look like concealment (lessons 14 and 15). An imperfect decision, logged with its reasons, is defensible.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Risk memos and exceptions: making someone own the decision
md: An exception is a decision with a name, a reason, compensating controls and an end date. Without all four it is just an unfixed vulnerability that someone has stopped looking at.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inside the search tree: selection, expansion, evaluation and backup
md: Backup is where look-ahead becomes knowledge: exact outcomes and value estimates deep in the tree are averaged into the root's $Q$ values, with the sign flipped at every ply so each player maximizes their own result. The visit counts that result are the improved policy the network imitates.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop
md: For any self-improvement claim, ask two questions: what outside the current model decides that a sample is good, and how often is it wrong? The loop can only improve as far as that signal is informative.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Other ways to shrink context: RAG compressors and soft compression
md: A summary can be wrong in ways deletion cannot: it may state something no document says. RECOMP's hand check found its own summaries less faithful than GPT-3.5's (80% versus 90% fully faithful on 30 sampled NQ summaries), and the paper notes LLMs hallucinate more when synthesizing several documents. If answers must be traceable to sources, prefer extraction.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Equifax and Spring4Shell: when the framework evaluates input
md: Equifax, Spring4Shell, ProxyLogon (lesson 14) and MOVEit all ended the same way: a **web shell** written into a directory the web server executes. Two cheap controls hit all of them: make web roots read-only to the app's own user, and alert on new script files appearing there.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Structured output today: grammar masks inside the SGLang scheduler
md: In SGLang a grammar costs three things: a compile per distinct schema (hidden by the cache after the first request), a CPU mask per request per step (hidden behind the forward pass by delaying only the sampling), and one decode step per forced token.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: A CH query must not stop the first time the two searches meet. The meeting node with the best sum may be found later. Each side stops only when its own queue minimum is at least the best sum found so far.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: A SIMD register is a small array of lanes. One instruction does the same operation on every lane. Lane count = register width / element width, so 4, 8 or 16 floats for 128, 256 or 512 bits. Vertical (lane-wise) work is cheap; horizontal (across-lane) work costs shuffles.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
md: Compile for what you can require, dispatch for what you cannot. -march levels give the compiler AVX2 or AVX-512 everywhere but crash on older CPUs; target_clones, __builtin_cpu_supports or is_x86_feature_detected! pick the best version per machine at run time.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: Colocation saves GPUs and keeps every GPU busy in a synchronous loop, but it forces phases to take turns and requires offloading. Separate pools only win if you also overlap rollout with training; on their own they just double the GPU count.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
md: Fully async needs separate rollout and training GPUs to overlap anything, and its README lists no evaluation mode (it would conflict with the continuously running model), so evaluate with a separate path or job. Importance-sampling corrections such as TIS (lesson 8) help with mismatch, but the docs say they do not justify an unlimited stale queue.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Consensus under attack: Sybil, 51 percent and eclipse attacks
md: Open networks defeat Sybil attacks by making votes cost a scarce resource (work or stake). The attacker's share sets the odds; confirmations and finality are how recipients buy safety.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Front-running, MEV and commit-reveal
md: Commit-reveal hides choices, not existence: observers still see that you committed and when. Without a reveal deadline and a rule for non-revealers (for example, forfeiting a deposit), a participant who dislikes the outcome can simply never reveal.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam
md: The CSRB's review of the group known as Lapsus$ found that, in a few cases, the attackers "impersonated help desk personnel over direct chat messages and encouraged employees to approve the MFA prompts". When you contact a user about an alert, use a channel the attacker cannot be sitting in, and teach users that the real SOC never asks them to approve a prompt.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Metrics, burnout and the analyst's ethics
md: The analyst's job, in one sentence: answer each alert with evidence, quickly and in order of risk, write it down so others can act and check, and use the access that makes this possible only for that purpose.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: SIM swaps, bribed insiders and people you do not employ
md: People outside your organisation (carrier staff, outsourced agents, contractors) can be the weak link for your accounts. Design so that no single outside person's mistake or bribe hands over a login, and make reporting approaches normal inside.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: Words to keep apart: a **latent** is a unit of the SAE; a **feature** is the concept you hope it captures. Gemma Scope says 'latents' for exactly this reason. A latent with a clean name is a hypothesis about a model feature, not proof of one. Lesson 5 shows how a latent gets its name and how that name is tested.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: High variance explained is not full understanding. Sonnet's SAEs explained at least 65% of variance, so a sizeable part of the activation lives in the error term, and a latent's top activating examples do not prove what it does. Use ablation or steering to check.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: The variogram turns Tobler's law into numbers: how much readings disagree, on average, as a function of distance. Its nugget, sill and range are what kriging uses to decide weights.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
md: Accept with $\min(1, p/q)$, on rejection sample from $\text{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$, where norm rescales to sum to 1. Accepted mass is $\min(p, q)$ and residual mass is $p - \min(p, q)$; they add up to $p$ for any draft.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
md: Mel settings are not interchangeable. librosa defaults to the Slaney scale, while `torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram` defaults to `mel_scale='htk'` and `n_mels=128`. Features computed with different settings than a model was trained on look like a different microphone to the model.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: The stack is not faster *memory*. Stack and heap bytes live in the same RAM behind the same caches. What is cheaper is *allocation*: one `sub` on `rsp` versus a search through allocator data structures. The top of the stack is also almost always hot in cache because it is reused constantly.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: Huge pages are not free. The THP documentation warns that a process that maps a large region but touches one byte can get a whole 2 MiB page instead of 4 KiB, and allocating a huge page needs 2 MiB of *physically contiguous* memory, which may require compaction: the kernel moves in-use pages around to assemble a free contiguous run. That is why `madvise` mode exists.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
md: LLM judges are convenient but not neutral. CAA used GPT-4 to score open-ended answers from 1 to 10 and notes the scores are sensitive to the rubric's wording; they spot-checked against their own ratings. String-matching refusal detectors have the opposite problem: they catch "I'm sorry" but not a harmful reply, so Arditi et al. paired them with Llama Guard 2.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Two different knobs, often confused. The bound $B$ moves the watermark (how long to wait before the first result). The allowed lateness $L$ keeps state after that (how long to accept corrections). Raising $B$ delays every result; raising $L$ costs state memory and extra firings but does not delay the first result.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Attention output for a position = softmax(its query dotted with every key, divided by the square root of d_k), used as weights on the value vectors. Every step is a matrix multiply or a row-wise softmax, so all positions are computed at once.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
md: One layer: attention adds a cross-position change, add & norm, the FFN adds a per-position change, add & norm. At inference the encoder runs once and the decoder runs once per output token, with beam search choosing among the most probable partial outputs.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: the full RSJ weight and query term counts
md: Reweighting alone rarely helps much: the survey says term reweighting is not in general an effective way to improve search, and that expanding the query with new terms has to be considered as well. With only a handful of judgments the counts are also noisy; the 0.5 added to each count keeps one judgment from producing an infinite weight, not from being wrong.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: Pre-LN vs post-LN is not cosmetic. Xiong et al. show that in the original post-LN Transformer the gradients near the output are large at initialization, which is why it needs a careful learning-rate warmup. Placing LayerNorm inside the residual branch, as GPT-2 does, gives well-behaved gradients at initialization.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
md: $f'(x)$ answers: if I nudge $x$ by a tiny amount, how many times that amount does $f$ change? Positive means $f$ rises to the right, negative means it falls, zero means the tangent is flat.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: The gradient gives the direction; the learning rate decides the distance. The largest stable learning rate is set by the **steepest** direction of the loss, while progress in the **shallowest** direction decides how long training takes.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
md: A command runs in a **copy** of the shell. It inherits open files, the working directory and exported variables, and nothing it changes flows back. Only builtins and functions run inside the shell itself.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
md: grep selects lines, sed rewrites them, awk computes over fields, and find selects files. Single-quote every pattern so the shell leaves it alone, and add `-E` when you want `+`, `?`, `|` or groups.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
md: An embedding is a learned weight matrix indexed by item ID. Meaning is not built in: the vectors start random and become useful only because some training objective rewards putting related items close together. The rest of this course is about which objectives do that.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Contrastive training in practice: in-batch negatives and collapse
md: A falling contrastive loss is not proof of a good representation: a model can solve the training task with features that transfer poorly, as SimCLR's normalization ablation shows. Track a downstream measure such as linear evaluation, and check for collapse by looking at the spread of the embeddings.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: Reserving the maximum length for every request wastes most of the cache. vLLM's profiling found only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory held actual token states in earlier systems, due to reserved slots and fragmentation. PagedAttention fixes this by allocating the cache in small fixed-size blocks, like OS pages.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: A **program** is a file of bytes on disk. A **process** is a running instance of it: its own memory (code, data, heap, stack), its own register values (the CPU's working slots, lesson 3), and OS bookkeeping such as open files. One program can be running as many processes at once.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: `call` = push return address + jump. `ret` = pop into the program counter. Everything a function keeps on the stack lives only until it returns, which is why the stack can be reused so cheaply.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
md: Same network, three different training signals: raw text (what comes next?), demonstrations (what would a good assistant write?), and comparisons (which of these two answers is better?). Each stage starts from the weights of the previous one.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback
md: AI feedback moves the specification, it does not remove it. The labels are only as good as the feedback model and the principles, and a model judging a model can share its blind spots. Teams still check AI-labeled preferences and the resulting policy against human judgments.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Analysis in depth: tokenizing, stemming and what normalizing costs
md: Analysis decides what a term is. Tokenizing and normalizing more aggressively makes more forms meet (recall) and more unrelated words collide (precision). Pick per language and domain, and apply the same chain to documents and queries.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Getting the top k fast: tiers, MaxScore and WAND
md: Inexact methods can drop a document that exhaustive scoring would rank in the top k, because the selection (champion lists, tiers, idf thresholds) is fixed before the query arrives. The textbook argues this is often acceptable, since cosine is itself only a proxy for relevance, but it is a quality trade, not a free speedup.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
md: A missing header in a prerequisite list gives silent stale builds. With `main.o: main.c` only, changing SQUARE to a cube in square.h rebuilt area.o alone, and app still printed 9 instead of 27. List every header, or let the compiler do it: `-MMD` makes GCC and Clang write a .d file of each source's user-header dependencies for the Makefile to include.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Every malloc needs exactly one matching free, on every path out of the function. Missing it leaks memory; doing it twice, or touching the block afterwards, is undefined behavior that can corrupt the allocator's own bookkeeping.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: 'It runs fine' is not evidence that C code is correct. A clean run without sanitizers says almost nothing about memory safety; even a clean sanitizer run covers only the paths your inputs exercised.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: Assigning, passing, or returning a non-`Copy` value moves it. To keep using the original, either `clone()` it (pay for a copy) or lend it out with a reference (next lesson).

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: `clone()` everywhere and `Rc<RefCell<T>>` everywhere make errors go away but give up what ownership buys you: clones cost time and memory, and `RefCell` turns compile-time guarantees into run-time panics. Reach for them when the data really has no single owner, not to silence the checker.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: Not every useful function is linear. $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \ne 0$ is **affine**: it moves the origin, so $f(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{b}$ instead of $\mathbf{0}$. Neural network layers are affine, and their activation functions (like ReLU, explained next) are not linear at all. That nonlinearity is what lets a deep network do more than one big matrix could.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The SVD: rotate, stretch, rotate, then keep what matters
md: Every matrix is rotate, stretch, rotate: $A = U\Sigma V^\top$. $\sigma_1$ is the spectral norm, $\sigma_1/\sigma_n$ the condition number, the count of nonzero $\sigma_i$ the rank. Truncating to the top $r$ terms is the best rank-$r$ approximation, and PCA is the SVD of centered data.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
md: Compute $\mu$ and $\sigma$ on the **training** data only and reuse those same numbers for validation, test and production inputs. Computing them on all the data leaks information from the held-out rows into training (lesson 11).

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Bias and variance: where the U-shaped test curve comes from
md: High variance is not the same as high training error. The degree-9 fit has zero training error and the largest variance; its errors show up only on new data.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: A hidden layer only adds power because of the nonlinearity between layers. Without it, any stack of layers is one linear map in disguise.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The cost of backprop: compute, activation memory, checkpointing
md: Backprop's compute is a small constant times the forward pass, about two more matrix multiplies per layer. Its memory is the real constraint: every activation from the forward pass stays alive until its layer's backward step, unless you pay compute to recompute it.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
md: The offset is never translated, and the page table is per process. Two processes can use the same virtual address 21 and reach completely different physical bytes; that is the isolation, not a bug.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
md: A deadlock-prone program can run correctly many times, because the deadlock needs an unlucky interleaving. Testing does not show it is safe; a lock order does.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive events ("sum is 2" and "sum is 12") cannot both happen, so learning one happened tells you the other did not: they are strongly *dependent*. Independence means the joint probability factorizes, $P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C)$.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
md: Noise in an average shrinks as $1/\sqrt n$. That single scaling law explains why larger batches give smoother gradients, why small evals are noisy, and why A/B tests need large samples to detect small effects.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
md: Every test in this lesson is the same move: estimate, compute its standard error from the variance rules and the CLT, and ask how many standard errors the estimate sits from the null. Significance depends on sample size as much as on effect size.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
md: Never report a scaling-law forecast without two checks: refit from several starts with tight tolerances and confirm they agree, and bootstrap the runs to get a range. A single unconverged fit can be off by 2x and still look perfectly reasonable.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
md: P@k does not average well across queries. If a query has only 3 relevant documents, even a perfect system gets P@10 = 0.3. Also note that trec_eval's P@k pads short result lists with nonrelevant documents: retrieving 15 documents with 4 relevant gives P@20 = 4/20 = 0.2.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Online evaluation: clicks, position bias, A/B tests and interleaving
md: Absolute online metrics compare different users at different times, so user variation swamps small quality differences. Interleaving shows both systems to the same user on the same query and asks which one they preferred, the online version of a paired test.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Chunking documents and adapting a model to your corpus
md: Keep the evaluation queries out of training. Generating synthetic queries over the whole corpus, test passages included, is fair: in production you have the corpus but not the users' queries. Training on the evaluation queries, or tuning until one small dev set looks good, is not.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
md: Byte-level BPE = UTF-8 bytes as the base alphabet (256 symbols, so nothing is ever unknown) + a regex pre-tokenizer that limits where merges can happen + an ordered merge list. Decoding concatenates bytes and is lossless.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
md: He et al. report that their 30-layer plain ReLU network trained with He initialization while the Xavier-initialized version *completely stalled*, with all gradients diminishing. Yet on their 22-layer model both converged (He init just started reducing error earlier), and on a smaller model the final accuracies were about the same. A bad init does not always crash; past some depth it silently stops learning.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
md: Log per step: loss, global gradient norm and learning rate. Log per layer: update-to-weight ratio (about 1e-3), activation std and dead fraction. Each failure in this course has a signature: shrinking scale with depth and ratios near 1e-8 for a bad init; ratios near 1e-2, dead units and a climbing gradient norm for too high a rate.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Product quantization by hand: codebooks, lookup tables, re-ranking
md: PQ stores m bytes per vector and estimates each distance with m table lookups. The estimates are good enough to build a shortlist, not to set the final order: keep the full vectors somewhere and re-rank the top few dozen.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Protestware: when the legitimate maintainer is the threat
md: Misconception: "Signed packages are safe packages." A signature answers 'did this come from the expected publisher, unmodified?'. It cannot answer 'does the publisher mean well?'. Protestware, and the xz backdoor (a trusted maintainer by then), passed every authenticity check.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: The Gaussian loop: unbiased fits that still shrink to a point
md: Sampling error makes each generation's fit a random step, and steps that multiply variance by a mean-one factor still shrink it in the typical run. Unbiased estimation does not save a closed loop.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What happens when your program calls write
md: Two traps in the convention. The 4th argument goes in `r10`, not `rcx` as in a normal C call, because the `syscall` instruction itself overwrites `rcx` with the return address. And after the call, `rcx` and `r11` are garbage from your point of view. Compilers know this; hand-written inline assembly must list them as clobbered.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
md: `munmap` can fail with `ENOMEM` even though it frees memory. mmap(2) explains why: unmapping a region in the middle of a mapping creates two smaller mappings, and that can exceed the per-process limit.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Why the average hides the requests users remember
md: Report latency as a distribution: several percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9) plus the maximum, not a mean. The mean blends a few terrible requests into many good ones and describes no actual user.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Signalling firewalls: message categories, home routing, monitoring
md: Signalling firewalls apply three ideas: some messages never belong on the interconnect, some may only come from the subscriber's home, and some must match where the subscriber actually is. Hiding the IMSI (home routing) makes the third kind much harder to abuse.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Salt Typhoon: espionage inside carrier networks (2024 to 2025)
md: Salt Typhoon worked through routers and management planes, not through exotic telecom protocols. Patch edge devices, keep management out of band, make a central copy the source of truth for configuration, and treat lawful-interception data as a prime target.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: *Present* and a missing end date are not the same thing. *Present* is an explicit claim of a current role. A blank end date may mean the person forgot to fill it in. Pick a convention, store which case occurred, and do not silently treat blanks as current.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
md: Repeated sampling scales **coverage** smoothly; selection without a reliable checker does not keep up. The useful question is never only how many samples, but how good is the verifier at the tail.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Sequential thinking lets later tokens build on earlier ones, which parallel sampling cannot. s1 found that majority voting over the base model could not catch up with the budget-forced fine-tuned model.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
